passage:
Family diary, Sunday. Irfan, Noor's abba.
Today the family group lit up again. Rehana's aunt forwarded a message about child kidnappers in vans "in every city". By lunch, three relatives had called Rehana, telling us never to take baby Noor outside. Ammi wanted to hire a guard. Meanwhile I noticed: the stair gate has been broken for a week, the cleaning liquids sit under the kitchen sink with no lock, and Noor's crib is right next to the window cord. Nobody mentioned those. What I did: I checked the city police's page; the forwarded message had been marked false last year. I asked the family, gently, whether anyone had real figures. Then I fixed the gate and moved the crib.

qa.q: What had been broken for a week?
qa.a: The stair gate had been broken for a week.

qa.q: What was Irfan worried about while the family panicked?
qa.a: Irfan worried that the vivid rumour was pulling everyone's attention away from real risks at home, like the broken gate, the unlocked cleaning liquids and the window cord near the crib.

qa.q: Which of Irfan's steps would help other families facing a scary forward?
qa.a: Checking the forward against an official source, asking whether anyone has real figures, and then fixing the ordinary hazards at home.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel after three worried calls from relatives?
qa.a: Rehana may feel scared and pressured by the calls, and then relieved when the message turns out to be false and the home becomes safer. 🙏

grounding: Shows a new father noticing relatives panic over a forwarded kidnapping rumour while ignoring everyday home dangers, and checking the real numbers.

passage:
Wednesday, 2 am feed done
Our daughter Mishti is three weeks old and my phone won't stop buzzing. My wife Parveen's mausi sent a voice note about a gang stealing newborns from hospitals, and now the whole family group is sure it's happening in our city. Ma wants us to keep the curtains shut all day. I felt my own chest tighten listening to it. But then, standing at the counter warming the bottle, I saw the kettle's cord hanging within reach of the baby bouncer, and the gas knob we keep forgetting to turn off. Nobody sends voice notes about those. Tomorrow I'll ask Ma, kindly, how many babies she actually knows were taken. And I'll tape the cord up.
Ujjwal

qa.a: She sent a voice note about a gang stealing newborns from hospitals.

passage: The rumour reached the village near Chitradurga by phone on a Tuesday: men in a white van were taking children from the fields. By evening Sahil's mother had locked the gate at five, and his aunt refused to let the children walk to the anganwadi. Sahil, holding his three-month-old daughter on the verandah, listened to the relatives on speaker. Everyone had forwarded the same message; no one knew where it came from. He looked around his own house. The kerosene tin by the stove. The old well behind the cowshed with a broken lid. His wife, Keerthana, said quietly, "The well frightens me more than any van." The next day Sahil went to the police outpost and asked if there had been any such case in the district. "None," the constable said. "Same message every monsoon." That afternoon, Sahil fixed the well lid.

qa.q: What did the rumour say was happening in the fields?
qa.a: Men in a white van were taking children from the fields.

qa.q: What was Sahil probably thinking as he looked around his own house?
qa.a: He was likely worried and starting to see that the real risks for his baby might be close at home, like the kerosene tin and the well, not the van in the forwarded message.

qa.q: Which choice by Sahil made his daughter safer?
qa.a: Checking the rumour at the police outpost instead of passing it on, and then fixing the broken well lid, a real everyday danger.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel when Sahil fixes the lid?
qa.a: She would likely feel heard and relieved, since she had said the well frightened her more than any van. 🙂

passage: In their Prague flat, Pavel was changing his son's nappy when his phone buzzed again. Jana's sister Camila had forwarded a message to the family group: strangers were snatching babies from prams in the city parks. "Don't take Matěj out alone!" By noon Jana's mother had called twice. Jana looked shaken. "Maybe we just stay in this week." Pavel wiped his hands and read the message again. No names, no dates, no source. He searched the police website: no reports of any such thing. Then he glanced around the room. The car seat they still hadn't fitted properly. The blind cord hanging near the cot. "I'm not saying we shouldn't be careful," he told Jana. "I'm saying let's be careful about the real stuff." That evening, instead of replying to the group, he fitted the car seat and tied up the cord.

Dear Usha akka,
Since you asked how the first months with baby Mihir are going: tiring, happy, and full of forwards. This week Amma's side of the family went into full panic over a message saying strangers in a grey van were taking babies from our district. Periamma called three times. Appa wanted to stop the nanny taking Mihir out in the pram. I checked with a friend at the district police office: there hasn't been a single case here this year. Meanwhile, the same relatives who were panicking keep leaving pills on the low table and hot tea on the edge of the bed where Mihir rolls. I said so, as gently as I could, and asked everyone to keep those up high. Amma sulked, then moved the tea.
Naveen, your very tired brother

qa.a: That there hasn't been a single case in the district this year.

passage: Damini, you asked what being a new dad is like. Honestly? It's mostly managing the family group. Last month someone forwarded a video of a masked man grabbing a child from a park, with "Happening in our city NOW" in red letters. By evening my mother had cancelled Esther's park walks, my aunt wanted a tracker in her booties, and my cousin called me careless for opening a window. I watched the video properly. The signs in it were in another language, and the same clip had been fact-checked two years ago. So I did the boring thing: I asked our local ward office how many children had gone missing in our area. Answer: none this year. What they did mention was falls from balconies. We have a balcony. Francis, the fun dad, spent Sunday putting up a grille.

passage: I became a father in March, and by May I noticed something in our family group chat. Every day, someone forwarded a message: a child kidnapped from a park, men in a white van, a video from somewhere unnamed. My aunt called Bidisha, my wife, in a panic. "Don't take the baby out!" Everyone was frightened. Meanwhile, at home, the same aunt had left her medicine box on the low table, and the balcony grill had a gap wide enough for a crawling baby. Nobody mentioned those. I felt uneasy, and a bit angry. So I looked up the police figures for our city. Kidnappings by strangers were very rare; most messages were old or false. Falls at home were far more common. I told the group, gently. Then I moved the medicine box to a high shelf and called a welder about the grill. I'm Jeevan, and I'm learning which worries to keep.

qa.a: Messages about a child kidnapped from a park and men in a white van.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel noticing the panic over forwards but not the home risks?

A Tuesday in July. Omkar's mother-in-law arrived at their Mumbai flat, clutching her phone. "A child was stolen from a hospital! It's on every group!" Leela, holding their two-month-old, went pale. Omkar watched the fear spread through the room.

That Friday. His mother-in-law now wouldn't let anyone take the baby to the building garden. But she kept leaving the hot iron on the edge of the bed, the cord dangling. Omkar noticed. He also noticed the kitchen floor wet and slippery near the baby's mat. He asked quietly, "Has anyone checked if this story is true? How often does this happen?"

The next Monday. Omkar had looked up the numbers. The story was two years old, from another state. He showed Leela and her mother. Then he said, "What scares me more is the iron." He fixed a hook for it on the wall. His mother-in-law, a little embarrassed, started unplugging it after use.

qa.q: Where was the child said to be stolen from?
qa.a: From a hospital.

passage: Pankaj, the family group is sending you kidnapping videos? Let me tell you what happened when your cousin was born. I was twenty-five, a new father in Guwahati. My uncles forwarded messages every day: kidnappers in white vans, children stolen from parks. My mother cried on the phone. She wanted the baby locked inside. I was scared too. But I noticed our house had a pond in the back with no fence, and the stairs had no railing. Nobody in the family talked about those. So I went to the police station and asked the officer: how many kidnappings here, really? He laughed and said almost none, and those were mostly family disputes. But drownings in small ponds, he said, happen every monsoon. I came home and built a fence that week. That's what Mridul learned: ask what the numbers say, then fix the real dangers.

Asif's son was three months old when the rumour reached his mother. A voice note was going around the colony: child-lifters in a white van, near the Mumbai markets. By evening, his mother and two aunts had decided the baby would not leave the flat for a month.

Asif listened from the kitchen doorway. He noticed his aunt holding the baby while pouring hot tea with the other hand. He noticed the pressure cooker hissing on the low stove. He noticed the ceiling fan's loose wiring, which he'd been meaning to fix since the baby was born.

He called Francis, his neighbour, a constable at the local police station. "Anything real about a white van?"

"Nothing. Same message went around two years ago. Fake."

Asif came back in. "Ammi, the police say it's a false message." Then he gently took the tea from his aunt, turned the cooker's handle inward, and went to find the electrician's number.

"I saw it, Tarun. Where did it come from?"

"Mausi sent it. It has a video."

"Of what?"

"A man grabbing a child."

"Where?"

"...It doesn't say."

"Let me search." Uday typed. "Tarun, this video is from another country, four years ago. The police here say the message is fake."

"But what if?"

"I hear you. I'm scared for Chinu too." Uday looked at his daughter, crawling on the floor. "But look at her now."

"What?"

"She's heading for the phone charger in the socket. The mop bucket's right there. And your bike keys are on the floor."

Tarun grabbed the keys. "Oh."

"Those happen every day in homes. The kidnapper story happens mostly in forwards."

"So what do we do?"

"Socket covers tomorrow. Bucket goes in the bathroom. And we ask Mausi to stop forwarding."

I'm Harish, and I became a father in March. Two weeks ago my family chat group exploded. Someone forwarded a message: a gang kidnapping babies in our city, dressed as vegetable sellers. No names, no dates, just capitals and exclamation marks.
My mother stopped letting the maid take my son to the park. My aunt called three times a day. My cousin Farhan said we should put a lock on the gate.
Meanwhile, in our own flat, the balcony railing had a gap wide enough for a toddler, medicines sat on a low shelf, and the geyser wire hung loose. Nobody had noticed those for months.
I asked Farhan, "What do the actual numbers say? How many kidnappings in our city this year?" He didn't know. I checked the police website. The rumour wasn't there.
So I spent Sunday fixing the balcony gap and moving the medicines up high. My mother watched, and slowly, she stopped forwarding the messages.

qa.a: He fixed the balcony gap and moved the medicines up high.
